quiz_title: Food Cost & Financial Management — Concept Revision Quiz
description: A set of concept-recall questions covering the substantive teaching content of the Food Cost Calculator lecture (financial metrics, food costing, menu pricing, daily/weekly monitoring, and special topics). The narrative 'Fun Version' retelling of the same material is intentionally excluded, as are the promotional Gold Membership details.

questions.question: According to the lecture, what is described as "the heart of the business"?
options: Marketing
Unit economics
Staff management
Customer service
questions.correct_answer: Unit economics
questions.explanation: The lecture opens by establishing unit economics as the central, non-negotiable foundation of a profitable business.

questions.question: What key distinction does the lecture draw between a for-profit business and charitable work?
options: For-profit businesses must track expenses more carefully
A for-profit business cannot systematically operate at a loss while serving customers
Charitable work doesn't need a business plan
There is no meaningful difference
questions.correct_answer: A for-profit business cannot systematically operate at a loss while serving customers
questions.explanation: Serving customers can't mean deliberately or systematically losing money if the venture is meant to be for-profit.

questions.question: Which statement best reflects the lecture's view on entrepreneurial skill?
options: An entrepreneur must personally master finance, cooking, marketing, and operations
An entrepreneur should recognise which capabilities the business needs and make sure the business has them — not necessarily do everything themselves
Delegation is a sign of weak leadership
Only large businesses can afford to delegate
questions.correct_answer: An entrepreneur should recognise which capabilities the business needs and make sure the business has them — not necessarily do everything themselves
questions.explanation: The key entrepreneurial skill is recognising required capabilities and ensuring the business has them, via employees, consultants, freelancers, or other specialists.

questions.question: In the revenue breakdown framework, what comes right after "Food, Gas & Packaging" is subtracted from Total Revenue?
options: Net Margin
Gross Margin
Rent
Operating Costs
questions.correct_answer: Gross Margin
questions.explanation: The chain is: Food + Gas + Packaging → Gross Margin → Rent + Employees + Marketing + Misc → Net Margin.

questions.question: How should the lecture's percentage benchmarks (e.g. 30% food cost, 70% gross margin) be treated?
options: As fixed rules every outlet must follow
As benchmarks/frameworks to adapt to your own location and business model
As legal requirements
As targets only relevant to large chains
questions.correct_answer: As benchmarks/frameworks to adapt to your own location and business model
questions.explanation: The lecture is explicit: these are frameworks, not rigid rules — actual performance depends on location, rent, and business model.

questions.question: Why might one tea outlet charge ₹20 for a cup while another charges only ₹10?
options: Different quality of tea leaves only
Differences in their cost structure, particularly rent
One outlet is simply more popular
Government price controls
questions.correct_answer: Differences in their cost structure, particularly rent
questions.explanation: A high-rent, high-street location can't necessarily sustain the same menu price as a low-rent location.

questions.question: If a business has high rent, what does the lecture suggest as ways to compensate?
options: Increase menu prices, increase sales volume, or otherwise adjust the cost structure
Reduce staff wages only
Stop tracking food cost
Move to a smaller kitchen
questions.correct_answer: Increase menu prices, increase sales volume, or otherwise adjust the cost structure
questions.explanation: Menu pricing must be compatible with the economics of the location.

questions.question: What is the "core principle" the lecture emphasises about financial management?
options: Achieving a predetermined set of percentages exactly
Continually understanding where the money is going, by monitoring Revenue → Food Cost → Gross Margin → Operating Costs → Profit
Copying competitor pricing
Minimising all costs regardless of quality
questions.correct_answer: Continually understanding where the money is going, by monitoring Revenue → Food Cost → Gross Margin → Operating Costs → Profit
questions.explanation: Financial management is about understanding where the money is going, not blindly hitting fixed percentages.

questions.question: Besides controlling costs, what other major benefit of calculating food cost does the lecture highlight?
options: It automatically increases sales
It helps detect wastage by comparing estimated vs. actual food-cost percentages
It eliminates the need for a POS system
It replaces the need for staff training
questions.correct_answer: It helps detect wastage by comparing estimated vs. actual food-cost percentages
questions.explanation: If estimated wastage is 5% but actual figures show 8–10%, that gap is a warning sign worth investigating.

questions.question: True or False: According to the lecture, improving food-cost control by even a small percentage can increase profit without needing more customers.
options: True
False
questions.correct_answer: True
questions.explanation: The same sales volume can become more profitable purely through better cost control.

questions.question: What does the lecture say a menu price should NOT be based only on?
options: Ingredient ratios
What competitors charge for a similar item
Local market prices
Wastage percentage
questions.correct_answer: What competitors charge for a similar item
questions.explanation: A menu price should not be determined only by looking at what competitors charge — it must reflect your own cost structure.

questions.question: For conservative costing, what pricing approach does the lecture recommend when costing an ingredient like onions?
options: Use the lowest price you can find
Use the maximum/current market price
Use last year's average price
Ignore ingredient price fluctuations
questions.correct_answer: Use the maximum/current market price
questions.explanation: Using the maximum/current market price keeps the costing conservative, so real costs don't come in higher than planned.

questions.question: Why does the lecture insist on calculating the actual cost of a menu item rather than estimating it?
options: Estimating is illegal
The exact figures depend on local purchase prices and recipe, so only actual calculation reveals the true cost
Estimating takes longer than calculating
Competitors always calculate exactly
questions.correct_answer: The exact figures depend on local purchase prices and recipe, so only actual calculation reveals the true cost
questions.explanation: "A cup of tea costs about ₹3" is only meaningful once you know exactly why it costs ₹3.

questions.question: What is the basic formula the lecture gives for turning food cost into a menu price?
options: Menu Price = Food Cost + GST
Menu Price = Food Cost ÷ Target Food-Cost %
Menu Price = Food Cost × 2
Menu Price = Food Cost − Wastage
questions.correct_answer: Menu Price = Food Cost ÷ Target Food-Cost %
questions.explanation: Dividing food cost by your target food-cost percentage gives the price needed to hit that target.

questions.question: What is "differential pricing" as described in the lecture?
options: Charging every customer a different price
Offering an inexpensive, smaller entry-level product alongside regular-priced options, without forcing every item to carry the same low price
Changing prices daily based on demand
Giving discounts to loyal customers only
questions.correct_answer: Offering an inexpensive, smaller entry-level product alongside regular-priced options, without forcing every item to carry the same low price
questions.explanation: E.g. a ₹10 classic/plain chai in a smaller serving size, alongside ₹15–18 specialty varieties.

questions.question: If a location can't support a higher price for its core beverage, what alternative strategy does the lecture suggest?
options: Lower the quality of ingredients
Use a lower-priced beverage as an entry product and compensate with higher-margin snacks or add-ons
Close the business
Ignore margin and focus on volume only
questions.correct_answer: Use a lower-priced beverage as an entry product and compensate with higher-margin snacks or add-ons
questions.explanation: A lower-margin beverage can be balanced by a higher-margin snack, keeping the overall mix healthy.

questions.question: When introducing a specialty/premium tea priced higher than the base tea, what pricing mistake does the lecture specifically warn against?
options: Pricing it exactly the same as the base tea
Simply doubling the base price
Pricing it lower than the base tea
Not offering a specialty variant at all
questions.correct_answer: Simply doubling the base price
questions.explanation: If the base tea is ₹10, the lecture suggests ₹13 or ₹15 for a specialty version — not jumping straight to ₹20.

questions.question: True or False: According to the lecture, menu pricing should consider your target customer, local purchasing power, competitor pricing, expected sales volume, location, and product quality — not just cost.
options: True
False
questions.correct_answer: True
questions.explanation: Pricing is a balance between what the customer is willing to pay and what the business needs to earn.

questions.question: Once you build a food-cost calculator for one menu item, what does the lecture say to do for other items?
options: Start over from scratch each time
Duplicate the format and swap in different ingredients — the same tool works for any recipe
Hire a separate accountant for each item
Use estimates instead of the calculator
questions.correct_answer: Duplicate the format and swap in different ingredients — the same tool works for any recipe
questions.explanation: If your menu has ten varieties of tea, create the calculation once and change only the ingredients that differ.

questions.question: What core sequence does the lecture describe for costing any recipe?
options: Recipe → Quantity of each ingredient → Ingredient price → Cost per serving → Wastage → Total food cost
Recipe → Menu design → Marketing → Sales
Ingredient price → Recipe → Profit → Marketing
Wastage → Recipe → Price → Sales
questions.correct_answer: Recipe → Quantity of each ingredient → Ingredient price → Cost per serving → Wastage → Total food cost
questions.explanation: This gives a standard, repeatable cost for each menu item.

questions.question: For a snack like bajji or bonda, how does the lecture say oil cost per piece should be calculated?
options: Estimate a flat rate per snack regardless of oil used
Divide the total oil cost by the number of pieces produced from that oil
Ignore oil cost since it's negligible
Charge oil cost only once per day
questions.correct_answer: Divide the total oil cost by the number of pieces produced from that oil
questions.explanation: Calculate how many pieces one litre of oil produces, then divide the oil cost by that number.

questions.question: For black tea costing, what does the lecture say should change compared to the standard milk-tea recipe?
options: Add more sugar
Remove the milk and use water alone
Use a different type of tea powder
Double the tea powder quantity
questions.correct_answer: Remove the milk and use water alone
questions.explanation: Black tea removes milk entirely and uses water (e.g. 100 ml) instead.

questions.question: What does the lecture recommend regarding accuracy on Day One of a new outlet's food-cost tracking?
options: Expect perfectly accurate numbers immediately
Accept that accurate food-cost numbers take time (often three to six months) to stabilise, while still starting to monitor right away
Wait six months before tracking anything
Use only monthly tracking from the start
questions.correct_answer: Accept that accurate food-cost numbers take time (often three to six months) to stabilise, while still starting to monitor right away
questions.explanation: Don't expect perfect numbers on day one, but also don't postpone monitoring indefinitely.

questions.question: What should a simple daily report include, according to the lecture?
options: Only total sales
Cash sales, digital payments, total sales, petty-cash expenses, and ingredient/other purchases
Only ingredient purchases
A full profit-and-loss statement
questions.correct_answer: Cash sales, digital payments, total sales, petty-cash expenses, and ingredient/other purchases
questions.explanation: Keep this in a simple Excel sheet — no need to start with complicated POS/restaurant-management systems.

questions.question: Which ingredients does the lecture say to focus on first when monitoring food cost?
options: All ingredients equally, no matter how minor
The core ingredients that make up most of the cost
Only packaging materials
Only ingredients that are wasted
questions.correct_answer: The core ingredients that make up most of the cost
questions.explanation: Focusing on core ingredients first keeps monitoring manageable without getting lost in minor items.

questions.question: What comparison does the lecture recommend making on a weekly basis?
options: Weekly consumption vs. weekly sales
Daily temperature vs. sales
Staff attendance vs. revenue
Rent vs. marketing spend
questions.correct_answer: Weekly consumption vs. weekly sales
questions.explanation: Comparing actual consumption against actual sales each week is the core monitoring habit.

questions.question: Along with purchases, what two stock figures are needed to calculate food consumed?
options: Opening stock and closing stock
Maximum stock and minimum stock
Wasted stock and sold stock
Ordered stock and delivered stock
questions.correct_answer: Opening stock and closing stock
questions.explanation: Food Consumed = Opening Stock + Purchases − Closing Stock.

questions.question: According to the lecture, why does weekly monitoring matter?
options: It's a legal requirement
It catches discrepancies and issues early, before they compound over a longer period
It replaces the need for any daily recording
It's only useful for large chains
questions.correct_answer: It catches discrepancies and issues early, before they compound over a longer period
questions.explanation: Weekly monitoring surfaces problems while they're still small and easy to correct.

questions.question: What does the lecture suggest about staff accountability and food-cost monitoring?
options: Monitoring has nothing to do with staff behaviour
Regularly tracking food cost creates accountability, since deviations from standard recipes or wastage become visible
Staff should never be told about food-cost targets
Accountability only matters for management, not staff
questions.correct_answer: Regularly tracking food cost creates accountability, since deviations from standard recipes or wastage become visible
questions.explanation: If staff use more milk than the recipe specifies, or wastage rises, monitoring makes that visible.

questions.question: What is the lecture's advice on starting a monitoring system?
options: Build the most complex, comprehensive system possible from day one
Start with a simple system (weekly first), and add complexity like monthly tracking later
Skip monitoring until the business is profitable
Only monitor once a year
questions.correct_answer: Start with a simple system (weekly first), and add complexity like monthly tracking later
questions.explanation: "Weekly first, monthly later" — keep the first system simple.

questions.question: Which of these correctly lists the lecture's 9-step basic operating cycle, in order?
options: Record sales → Record purchases/expenses → Track opening/closing stock → Calculate consumption → Calculate food cost % → Compare with target → Investigate discrepancies → Correct the problem → Repeat every week
Record sales → Set menu prices → Hire staff → Advertise → Repeat monthly
Calculate profit → Record sales → Advertise → Repeat
Track stock → Set prices → Ignore wastage → Repeat annually
questions.correct_answer: Record sales → Record purchases/expenses → Track opening/closing stock → Calculate consumption → Calculate food cost % → Compare with target → Investigate discrepancies → Correct the problem → Repeat every week
questions.explanation: This nine-step cycle is described as the foundation of food-cost management.

questions.question: What is the formula for Food Cost %, as given in the lecture?
options: Food Consumed − Sales
Food Consumed ÷ Sales × 100
Sales ÷ Food Consumed × 100
Food Consumed × Sales
questions.correct_answer: Food Consumed ÷ Sales × 100
questions.explanation: This is one of the key numbers to remember from the lecture.

questions.question: What is the formula for Gross Margin, as given in the lecture?
options: 100% − Food-Cost %
Food Cost % + 100%
Food Cost % × 2
Sales − Food Cost
questions.correct_answer: 100% − Food-Cost %
questions.explanation: Gross margin is simply the complement of your food-cost percentage.

questions.question: How does the lecture describe inventory such as tea powder, flasks, and sugar held for ongoing operations?
options: It should be fully included in each item's food-cost calculation
It should be treated as working capital, separate from an individual menu item's food-cost calculation
It should be ignored entirely
It should only be counted once a year
questions.correct_answer: It should be treated as working capital, separate from an individual menu item's food-cost calculation
questions.explanation: Inventory/working capital ≠ food-cost calculation for an individual menu item — don't dump the value of all inventory into a single item's costing.

questions.question: What caution does the lecture give regarding the ₹20 lakh GST threshold mentioned in the source material?
options: It's a universal rule that applies to every business
It should not be treated as a universal rule — GST treatment depends on the nature of the business, registration, turnover, and other factors, so current rules should be checked
GST never applies to food businesses
The threshold guarantees GST exemption for all small businesses
questions.correct_answer: It should not be treated as a universal rule — GST treatment depends on the nature of the business, registration, turnover, and other factors, so current rules should be checked
questions.explanation: Always check the current GST rules applicable to your business and location rather than relying on a single rule of thumb.

questions.question: What does the lecture say about milk-fat proportion when preparing tea?
options: The milk proportion is always fixed regardless of fat content
With higher-fat milk (e.g. 6% fat), a lower proportion of milk is used than with lower-fat milk (e.g. 4.5% fat), and the exact ratio depends on taste and customer expectations
Fat content has no effect on the recipe
Only 4.5% fat milk should ever be used
questions.correct_answer: With higher-fat milk (e.g. 6% fat), a lower proportion of milk is used than with lower-fat milk (e.g. 4.5% fat), and the exact ratio depends on taste and customer expectations
questions.explanation: An example of adjusting a recipe according to ingredient characteristics, rather than applying one fixed rule.
